claims.claim: A good hearty laugh is good for the soul.
Good food and drink are gifts meant to be enjoyed.

stances.summary: This life is a time for sorrow over sin, not for laughing and joking. Christ is often seen weeping in the Gospels but never laughing, and play is the devil's gift, not God's.
stances.quote: For this is not the theatre for laughter, neither did we come together for this intent, that we may give way to immoderate mirth, but that we may groan, and by this groaning inherit a kingdom.
stances.translation: George Prevost, revised by M.B. Riddle, NPNF First Series vol. 10, 1888
stances.context: Same homily, a few lines earlier: Christ is seen weeping 'but nowhere laugh, nay, nor smile but a little; no one at least of the evangelists has mentioned this', and just after: 'For it is not God that grants to play, but the devil.' He adds one qualification: 'these things I say, not to suppress all laughter, but to take away dissipation of mind.' He says it again, more sharply, in Homily 15 on Hebrews, section 8 (Gardiner, NPNF1 vol. 14, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/240215.htm): 'Tell me, do you laugh? Where do you hear of Christ doing this? Nowhere'. That sermon also scolds people who laugh in church during the prayers. Preached at Antioch about 390, as a priest. Orthodox.

stances.summary: A believer has no time for laughter while so many are dead in sin and ought to be mourned. At most, a quiet cheerful smile is allowed. Loud laughter that shakes the body shows a soul not under control.
stances.quote: Since the Lord condemns those that laugh it is obvious that there is never a time of laughter for the believer, especially when there is so great a multitude of those who by transgression of the law dishonour God and are dead in sins, for whom one should mourn and grieve.
stances.translation: W.K.L. Clarke, The Ascetic Works of Saint Basil (London: SPCK, 1925), p. 241
stances.location: Question 31, 'Must we not laugh at all?' (Rufinus's Latin no. 58)
stances.context: The url is the archive.org text of a scanned book, so the quote runs across line breaks: compare after collapsing whitespace. Long Rules 17 (same file, pp. 180-181) is headed 'That it is necessary also to refrain from laughter'. It allows 'merriment to the extent of a cheerful smile', forbids 'loud laughter', and says the Lord seems 'never to have made use of laughter, so far as we may judge from the narrative of the gospels'. It also grants that Scripture sometimes uses 'laughter' to mean spiritual joy. These rules were written for ascetic communities, about 358-370. Irony worth knowing: Gregory of Nazianzus, his closest friend, praised Basil's own wit (see Gregory's entry).

stances.summary: Jokes may sometimes be pleasant, but they do not belong in a clergyman's life. We should avoid not only coarse jokes but joking of every kind, because laughing here leads to weeping hereafter.
stances.quote: Do we seek for something to laugh at, that laughing here we may weep hereafter? I think we ought to avoid not only broad jokes, but all kinds of jests, unless perchance it is not unfitting at the time for our conversation to be agreeable and pleasant.
stances.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, NPNF Second Series vol. 10, 1896
stances.work: On the Duties of the Clergy (De officiis ministrorum)
stances.context: Just before (1.23.102): 'For though at times jests may be proper and pleasant, yet they are unsuited to the clerical life. For how can we adopt those things which we do not find in the holy Scriptures?' It is addressed to his clergy, about 390, and modelled on Cicero's De officiis, which had allowed tasteful jokes. At 1.20.85 he also warns that frequent banquets and jests 'enervate that manly gravity'. Orthodox bishop.

stances.summary: Words that stir up laughter are banned everywhere in the monastery. Humility shows in not being quick to laugh.
stances.quote: But as for buffoonery or idle words, such as move to laughter, we utterly condemn them in every place, nor do we allow the disciple to open his mouth in such discourse.
stances.translation: D. Oswald Hunter Blair, The Rule of St. Benedict, 3rd ed. (Fort Augustus: Abbey Press, 1914)
stances.original: Scurrilitates vero vel verba otiosa et risum moventia aeterna clusura in omnibus locis damnamus et ad talia eloquia aperire os non permittimus. (as printed at https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/benedict.html)
stances.context: archive.org OCR text: compare after collapsing whitespace. The same Rule, chapter 4, tools 54-55: 'Not to speak vain words or such as move to laughter. Not to love much or excessive laughter.' Chapter 7, tenth degree of humility: 'that he be not easily moved and prompt to laughter', citing 'The fool lifteth up his voice in laughter'; eleventh degree: speak 'without laughter'. Chapter 7 draws on Cassian, Institutes 4.39. About 530-540. Written for monks.

stances.summary: Leave laughing and joking to worldly people. A consecrated Christian should be serious, though feelings can only be governed, never uprooted.
stances.quote: Leave to worldlings the privileges of laughing and being laughed at. One who is in your position ought to be serious.
stances.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, NPNF Second Series vol. 6, 1893
stances.context: Written in 414 to a young noblewoman who had just vowed virginity. He goes straight on to say that Cato 'laughed only once in his life', perhaps only to gain a reputation, and that 'we can but restrain and regulate our affections and passions; we cannot wholly extirpate them.' Irony worth knowing: Jerome was the sharpest satirist among the Fathers, and his letters and polemics mock opponents freely. Orthodox.

stances.summary: A holy person's face shows a steady heavenly gladness, not bursts of laughter, anger or grief. Martin was always the same.
stances.quote: No one ever saw him enraged, or excited, or lamenting, or laughing; he was always one and the same: displaying a kind of heavenly happiness in his countenance, he seemed to have passed the ordinary limits of human nature.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts, NPNF Second Series vol. 11, 1894
stances.original: Nemo umquam illum vidit iratum, nemo commotum, nemo maerentem, nemo ridentem: unus idemque fuit semper, caelestem quodammodo laetitiam vultu praeferens (https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/sulpiciusseverusmartin.html)
stances.work: Life of St Martin, by Sulpicius Severus
stances.context: This is not Martin's own words. It is a description by Sulpicius Severus, who knew him and wrote about 396, before Martin died. It is Martin's recorded manner, not a teaching he argued for, so strength 1. Note the pairing: no laughter, but constant 'heavenly happiness'.

stances.summary: Foolish mirth is one of the offspring of gluttony. It belongs with scurrility and babbling, not with the virtues.
stances.quote: From gluttony are propagated foolish mirth, scurrility, uncleanness, babbling, dulness of sense in understanding.
stances.translation: Library of the Fathers translation, Morals on the Book of Job (Oxford: J.H. Parker, 1844-1850)
stances.work: Moralia in Job (Morals on the Book of Job)
stances.context: This is part of his famous list of the seven principal vices and their offspring. It is a passing classification, and it is qualified by 'foolish', so strength 1. In the Pastoral Rule, Book 3, chapter 4 (Barmby, NPNF2 vol. 12, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/36013.htm), the cheerful are to be warned with 'Woe unto you that laugh now!', and 'the joyful have lechery close at hand'. This shows how the tradition linked laughter with gluttony, which ties the two claims of this topic together. Written about 578-595.

stances.summary: Keep away from people who love laughing and mockery, because they pull you into a lax life.
stances.quote: Be not friends with one that loves laughter and derision
stances.translation: A.J. Wensinck, Mystic Treatises by Isaac of Nineveh (Amsterdam, 1923)
stances.location: Wensinck's Treatise 50, 'Short sections containing various considerations'
stances.context: The sentence continues 'for he will drag thee towards lax customs', but the OCR puts a stray mark after 'derision', so the quote stops there. He adds: 'Be not joyous with him whose behaviour is lax; but be cautious against hating him.' In Treatise 60 he says of the saints: 'They weep, and the world laughs. They are sorry, and the world is joyful.' Isaac was a 7th-century East Syriac monk and bishop of Nineveh, of the Church of the East, and is venerated by the Orthodox. Wensinck translated from the Syriac.

stances.summary: Laughing without restraint is one of the ways worldly people break self-control, even when they think they are temperate.
stances.quote: Among people in the world, too, self-control seems to be practised, but folly lives alongside it, because they sin with all their other senses: they look about shamelessly and they laugh without restraint.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek alphabetical Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Cotelier text, PG 65)
stances.original: Καὶ γὰρ παρὰ τοῖς κοσμικοῖς σωφροσύνη δοκεῖ πολιτεύεσθαι, ἀλλὰ συμπάρεστιν αὐτῇ καὶ ἀφροσύνη, διὰ τὸ ταῖς ἄλλαις πάσαις αἰσθήσεσιν ἁμαρτάνειν. Καὶ γὰρ ὁρῶσιν ἀπρεπῶς, καὶ γελῶσιν ἀτάκτως.
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Apophthegmata Patrum), alphabetical collection
stances.context: The page prints the Greek next to Benedicta Ward's English. Ward's wording is copyrighted and is not used here. Her saying opens: 'We who have chosen this way of life must obtain perfect temperance'. Laughter is mentioned in passing as a sign of intemperance, so strength 1. The Sayings were compiled late in the 5th century from oral tradition. Syncletica was a 4th-century Egyptian ascetic.

stances.summary: If you laugh and chatter with people outside, you cannot expect to find peace when you go back inside. Guard yourself inside and out.
stances.quote: The old man said to him: Do you want to go out of your cell and find people laughing and laugh too, and find people talking and talk too, and then go into your cell and find yourself as you were? The brother said: What then? And the old man answered: Keep watch within; keep watch without.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek alphabetical Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Cotelier text, PG 65)
stances.original: Λέγει αὐτῷ ὁ γέρων· Θέλεις, ἐὰν ἐξέλθῃς ἐκ τοῦ κελλίου σου, καὶ εὕρῃς τοὺς γελῶντας, καὶ σὺ γελάσαι· καὶ τοὺς λαλοῦντας, καὶ σὺ λαλῆσαι· καὶ εἰσέλθῃς εἰς τὸ κελλίον σου, καὶ εὕρῃς ἑαυτὸν ὡς ἦς; Λέγει ὁ ἀδελφός· Ἀλλὰ τί; Καὶ ἀποκριθεὶς ὁ γέρων εἶπεν· Ἔσω τήρει φυλακήν, ἔξω τήρει φυλακήν.
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Apophthegmata Patrum), alphabetical collection
stances.context: Careful: this is a saying Poemen passes on ('Abba Poemen said that a brother asked Abba Simon...'). The answer is Simon's, and Poemen hands it on as teaching. It is weaker evidence for Poemen's own view, so strength 1. The page's English is Ward's (copyrighted, not used). Compiled late in the 5th century.

stances.summary: A monk's face should not break into laughter. Pambo's only recorded laugh was at the devils, mocking how weak they were.
stances.quote: They used to say that the face of Abba Panbo never smiled or laughed.
stances.translation: E.A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2 (London: Chatto & Windus, 1907), from the Syriac of 'Anan-Isho
stances.work: Sayings of the Fathers (Syriac collection of 'Anan-Isho), in Budge's Paradise
stances.location: Chapter 'Of scrupulous watchfulness in our thoughts and words and deeds', no. 325
stances.context: archive.org OCR with doubled spaces: compare after collapsing whitespace. Budge spells the name 'Panbo'. The story goes on: the devils carried a feather on a stick and danced, Pambo laughed, and when they cried that he had laughed, he said he 'laughed at your weakness', because it took so many of them to carry a feather. So the one laugh in the story is mockery of evil, like Tertullian's 'truth may laugh'. Pambo is not in the results pool. He was a 4th-century monk of Nitria.

stances.summary: Laughing is natural to human beings and should not be rooted out. It should be governed. A gentle smile that eases the strain of serious work is good. A guffaw or a giggle is not, and neither is being a professional joker.
stances.quote: For man is not to laugh on all occasions because he is a laughing animal, any more than the horse neighs on all occasions because he is a neighing animal. But as rational beings, we are to regulate ourselves suitably, harmoniously relaxing the austerity and over-tension of our serious pursuits, not inharmoniously breaking them up altogether.
stances.translation: William Wilson, ANF vol. 2, 1885
stances.context: The whole chapter is about laughter. 'Pleasantry is allowable, not waggery.' 'Whatever things are natural to men we must not eradicate from them, but rather impose on them limits and suitable times.' 'One needs not be gloomy, only grave.' He also allows that old men may joke with the young to encourage them. On the other side he calls a man's guffaw 'savage and insulting laughter' and says professional jokers are to be 'ejected from our society'. Written about 190-200, for lay Christians in the city, not for monks. This is the clearest real middle voice.

stances.summary: Some nonsense deserves to be laughed at rather than answered seriously. Truth is joyful and unafraid, so it may laugh. Decent laughter is even a duty.
stances.quote: Even the truth may indulge in ridicule, because it is jubilant; it may play with its enemies, because it is fearless. Only we must take care that its laughter be not unseemly, and so itself be laughed at; but wherever its mirth is decent, there it is a duty to indulge it.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts, ANF vol. 3, 1885
stances.original: congruit et veritati ridere quia laetans, de aemulis suis ludere quia secura est. curandum plane ne risus eius rideatur si fuerit indignus. ceterum ubicumque dignus risus, officium est. (https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.valentinianos.shtml)
stances.context: This laughter is ridicule aimed at a heresy, not laughter for rest or fun, so strength 1. The same chapter says 'Vain and silly topics are met with special fitness by laughter.' It was written about 206-208, when Tertullian was already leaning towards Montanism (later judged heterodox). Elsewhere he is severe about shows and pleasures (On the Spectacles).

stances.summary: When a listener is worn out, a good teacher wakes him up with something light and pleasantly cheerful, then carries on. A tired mind needs refreshing.
stances.quote: it becomes our duty to refresh his mind by saying something seasoned with an honest cheerfulness and adapted to the matter which is being discussed
stances.translation: S.D.F. Salmond, NPNF First Series vol. 3, 1887
stances.original: aut renovare oportet ejus animum, dicendo aliquid honesta hilaritate conditum et aptum rei quae agitur (https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/augustine/catechizandis.shtml)
stances.work: On the Catechising of the Uninstructed (De catechizandis rudibus)
stances.context: The setting is a listener who 'gapes and yawns'. The book's whole theme is teaching 'with cheerfulness' (hilaritas), and chapters 10-14 are about gaining it. In an early dialogue, On Music 2.14.26 (about 387-391), Augustine writes: 'it is wise now and then to relax the mind's edge that is rightly bent on tasks' (own rendering of 'Placet hoc nam sapienter, remittere interdum / aciem rebus agendis decenter intentam', https://www.augustinus.it/latino/musica/musica_2_libro.htm). Aquinas later used that line to defend jokes and games. Neither passage praises loud laughter as such, so strength 1. Orthodox.

stances.summary: Relaxing and being merry with the brothers is not a lapse. A bow that is always bent will snap, and so will people pushed too hard, so now and then you must come down to meet them.
stances.quote: The old man said to him: So it is also in the work of God. If we stretch the brothers beyond measure, they quickly break. So one must, now and then, come down to meet the brothers.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek alphabetical Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Cotelier text, PG 65)
stances.original: εἶδε τὸν ἀββᾶν Ἀντώνιον χαριεντιζόμενον μετὰ τῶν ἀδελφῶν ... Λέγει αὐτῷ ὁ γέρων· Οὕτως καὶ εἰς τὸ ἔργον τοῦ Θεοῦ· ἐὰν πλεῖον τοῦ μέτρου τείνωμεν κατὰ τῶν ἀδελφῶν, ταχὺ προσρήσσουσι. Χρὴ οὖν μίαν μίαν συγκαταβαίνειν τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς.
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Apophthegmata Patrum), alphabetical collection
stances.context: The setup: a hunter in the desert 'saw Abba Antony being playful (charientizomenon, joking) with the brothers' and was shocked. Antony had him draw his bow again and again until the hunter said it would break. The page's English is Ward's (copyrighted, not used). The same parable is told of St John the Evangelist and a hunter in Cassian, Conference 24.21 (see Cassian's entry), so it is a travelling story. The Sayings were compiled late in the 5th century, about a century after Antony. Athanasius's Life of Antony 67 (Ellershaw, NPNF2 vol. 4, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/2811.htm) adds that 'from the joy of his soul he possessed a cheerful countenance'. The saying defends merriment and rest, not hearty laughter as such.

stances.summary: Wit and light moments are good when used in the right season and without excess. His friend Basil was delightful company, kindly in his stories and refined in his wit, and was no buffoon.
stances.quote: Who was more kindly in his stories, more refined in his wit, more tender in his rebukes? His reproofs gave rise to no arrogance, his relaxation to no dissipation, but avoiding excess in either, he made use of both in reason and season, according to the rules of Solomon, who assigns to every business a season.
stances.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, NPNF Second Series vol. 7, 1894
stances.work: Oration 43, Funeral Oration on Basil the Great
stances.context: Gregory's own voice, about 381. In the same passage he defends Basil for not being 'a chatterer, and jester' and scorns stage-players who 'raise a laugh'. So he approves wit and relaxation in their season, not clowning. Gregory also wrote playful, teasing letters to Basil (Letters 4-6) and many poems. It is a telling contrast with Basil's own Rules against laughter. Orthodox.

stances.summary: The mind needs some recreation now and then, or it loses its strength. Even an apostle relaxed. A humble monk, though, is not quick to laugh.
stances.quote: do not let this slight and short relaxation of my mind disturb you, as unless it sometimes relieved and relaxed the rigour of its purpose by some recreation, the spirit would lose its spring owing to the unbroken strain, and would be unable when need required, implicitly to follow what was right.
stances.translation: Edgar C.S. Gibson, NPNF Second Series vol. 11, 1894
stances.location: Conference 24 (Abba Abraham), chapter 21, 'How the Evangelist John is said to have shown the value of relaxation'
stances.context: The words are put in St John the Evangelist's mouth, who was stroking a tame partridge when a philosopher dressed as a hunter mocked him. Abba Abraham tells the story in a Conference that Cassian wrote up about 426-429. Against it, Institutes 4.39 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/350704.htm) lists as the tenth sign of humility 'if he is not easily moved or too ready to laugh', which Benedict later copied. So Cassian holds both: recreation yes, easy laughter no. Cassian is honoured as a saint in the East, but his teaching on grace was criticised in the West.

stances.summary: Bodily laughter fights against humility more than anything. But God does not want us to mourn out of pain. He wants us, out of love, to rejoice in the laughter of the soul.
stances.quote: God does not ask or wish, my friends, that a man should mourn out of pain of heart, but rather that out of love for Him he should rejoice with the laughter of the soul.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek (PG 88) as transcribed on Greek Wikisource
stances.original: Οὐ δέεται, ὦ οὗτοι, οὐδὲ βούλεται Θεὸς ἄνθρωπον ἐξ ὀδύνης καρδίας πενθεῖν· ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον ἐξ ἀγάπης πρὸς αὐτὸν ἐν γέλωτι ψυχῆς ἀγάλλεσθαι.
stances.context: The same step says (own rendering): 'If nothing goes together with humility as mourning does, surely nothing opposes it as laughter does' (Εἰ οὐδὲν οὕτω τῇ ταπεινοφροσύνῃ ὡς τὸ πένθος συνέρχεται, οὐδὲν πάντως αὐτῇ ὡς ὁ γέλως ἀνθέστηκεν). It also says whoever wears blessed mourning 'has come to know the spiritual laughter of the soul' (τὸν τῆς ψυχῆς πνευματικὸν ἐγνώρισε γέλωτα). His key word is charmolype, 'joy-bearing sorrow'. So he rejects bodily laughter and praises an inner one. Written about 600 at Sinai. The Wikisource page adds bracketed note numbers such as (4) and (5), which are not part of the text. The only English versions are modern (Lazarus Moore 1959 and later), so none is used.

stances.summary: Put away sadness and put on cheerfulness, which always pleases God. A cheerful person does good, while a gloomy one grieves the Holy Spirit.
stances.quote: For every cheerful man does what is good, and minds what is good, and despises grief
stances.translation: F. Crombie, ANF vol. 2, 1885
stances.context: Just before: 'put on cheerfulness, which always is agreeable and acceptable to God, and rejoice in it.' The word is cheerfulness (hilaritas), not laughter, so strength 1. Roman, early to mid 2nd century, widely read in the early Church. Hermas is not in the results pool, but he is the earliest strong 'pro-cheerfulness' voice.

stances.summary: The Christian love-feast is a real meal shared with the poor. People eat enough to satisfy hunger and drink what befits the chaste, then pray.
stances.quote: As much is eaten as satisfies the cravings of hunger; as much is drunk as befits the chaste.
stances.translation: S. Thelwall, ANF vol. 3, 1885
stances.context: Written about 197, in his catholic period, to defend the Christian supper (agape) against pagan slander. It is a generous but sober picture of a shared meal: 'with the good things of the feast we benefit the needy'. Compare his second entry below. Some 10-20 years later, as a Montanist, he mocked the same Catholic love-feasts.

stances.summary: The mainstream Christians who feast and refuse strict fasts have made their stomach their god. Their kitchens have become their religion.
stances.quote: For to you your belly is god, and your lungs a temple, and your paunch a sacrificial altar, and your cook the priest, and your fragrant smell the Holy Spirit, and your condiments spiritual gifts, and your belching prophecy.
stances.translation: S. Thelwall, ANF vol. 4, 1885
stances.work: On Fasting, Against the Psychics (De ieiunio)
stances.context: Written after 210, in his Montanist period (heterodox). The whole treatise attacks the 'psychics', his name for Catholic Christians. Chapter 17: 'with you love shows its fervour in sauce-pans, faith its warmth in kitchens, hope its anchorage in waiters'. This is a later, harsher view than Apology 39 (his first entry). It is a change of tone that goes with his break with the Church.

stances.summary: Wine and rich food feed lust. A young woman consecrated to Christ should avoid wine like poison and eat simply. Abstinence brings us back to the Paradise that full stomachs lost.
stances.quote: I would begin by urging you and warning you as Christ's spouse to avoid wine as you would avoid poison. For wine is the first weapon used by demons against the young.
stances.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, NPNF Second Series vol. 6, 1893
stances.context: Written in 384 to a consecrated virgin. Section 10: 'Care must be taken, therefore, that abstinence may bring back to Paradise those whom satiety once drove out.' He adds qualifications. Section 11: God does not delight 'in a rumbling and empty stomach'; fasting is a means to chastity. Section 37 warns fasters against pride: 'another eats and wears a smiling face... He uses food in moderation and gives God thanks.' In Against Jovinian 2.16 he writes: 'we praise every creature of God, and yet prefer leanness to corpulence, abstinence to luxury, fasting to fullness.' His great opponent on this was Jovinian (see below).

stances.summary: Every food God made is good and may be tasted with thanks. But the aim of eating is to keep alive, not to enjoy it, so we should use cheap, plain food and avoid what only gives pleasure.
stances.quote: Nor indeed should we make pleasure the end of eating, but utility in order to preserve life
stances.translation: W.K.L. Clarke, The Ascetic Works of Saint Basil (London: SPCK, 1925), p. 183
stances.location: Question 19, 'What is the measure of continence?'
stances.context: archive.org OCR text: compare after collapsing whitespace. Long Rule 18 ('That it is necessary to eat all that is set before us') says monks should taste every kind of food when it is set before them, 'to show to the onlookers that to the pure all things are pure', against those who reject foods as evil. But they should still use 'the cheaper foods and bare necessaries', 'refraining entirely from what ministers to pleasure'. Long Rule 17 adds that the continent Christian is marked by 'emaciation of body and paleness'. Written for ascetic communities, about 358-370.

stances.summary: Food is good, and the fault is never in the food but in craving it. Still, he eats as one takes medicine, because the pleasure that comes with eating is a trap that tries to pass itself off as health.
stances.quote: This much have You taught me, that I should bring myself to take food as medicine.
stances.translation: J.G. Pilkington, NPNF First Series vol. 1, 1887
stances.context: Written about 397-400. The same chapter says 'whereas health is the reason of eating and drinking, there joins itself as an hand-maid a perilous delight'. At 10.31.46 he writes: 'It is not the uncleanness of meat that I fear, but the uncleanness of lusting.' Qualification: On Christian Doctrine 3.12.19 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/12023.htm) says 'a wise man may use the daintiest food without any sin of epicurism or gluttony'. Underneath it all is his rule, in On Christian Doctrine book 1, that only God is to be enjoyed (frui) and created things are to be used (uti). Marked 'disagree' because he explicitly refuses to make enjoyment the point, though he is not against food. Orthodox.

stances.summary: Taste is the most deeply rooted pleasure and the mother of the others, so watch it most closely. Let need, not pleasure, set how much you eat. Do not refuse the sweetness that comes with meeting a need, but never make it the aim.
stances.quote: To secure for the body a continuous tranquillity, unstirred by the pains of surfeit, we must make up our minds to a more sparing regimen, and constitute the need of it on each occasion not the pleasure of it, as the measure and limit of our indulgence.
stances.translation: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson, NPNF Second Series vol. 5, 1893
stances.context: Just before: 'above all to be specially watchful against the pleasure of taste... the mother as it were of all forbidden enjoyment'. Just after, a real qualification: 'we must not because of the resulting enjoyment reject the satisfaction, nor yet make this latter our leading aim. In everything we must select the expedient quantity, and leave untouched what merely feasts the senses.' Chapter 22 warns against the opposite excess of over-strict fasting. Written about 371. Macrina, his sister, left no surviving statement on food; the Life of Macrina shows her household sharing the same plain table.

stances.summary: Keep Christ's feast in the spirit, not with fine wines, clever cooking and luxury. Anything beyond real need is excess, above all while others go hungry.
stances.quote: let us not strive to outdo each other in intemperance (for to my mind every superfluity is intemperance, and all which is beyond absolute need) — and this while others are hungry and in want, who are made of the same clay and in the same manner.
stances.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, NPNF Second Series vol. 7, 1894
stances.work: Oration 38, On the Theophany (the Nativity of Christ)
stances.context: A Christmas sermon (Constantinople, 380). Just before: 'Let us not appraise the bouquet of wines, the kickshaws of cooks, the great expense of ointments.' The feast itself is kept joyfully, but the joy is to be spiritual. The claim that care for the hungry makes luxury wrong is part of his argument. Compare his lighter side on laughter (claim a). Orthodox.

stances.summary: The pleasures of taste were not made for us to enjoy. They were made as a test for virtue to overcome, and they are snares that lead to death.
stances.quote: Perhaps some one will say, Why, then, have these things been made, except that we may enjoy them? However, it has often been said that there would have been no virtue unless it had things which it might overpower.
stances.translation: William Fletcher, ANF vol. 7, 1886
stances.location: Book 6, chapter 22, 'Of the Pleasures of Taste and Smell'
stances.context: This is the most direct answer to the claim anywhere in the early sources. He poses the exact question and says no. The chapter ends: 'those enjoyments are to be guarded against, as snares or nets'. Written about 303-311 by a Latin rhetorician who became a Christian and later tutored Constantine's son. Orthodox in intent, though a layman and not a precise theologian.

stances.summary: A full stomach and a love of comfort shut out prayer and the love of God. Hunger and an empty stomach keep the mind clear and chaste.
stances.quote: A full stomach shrinks from examining spiritual questions, as a harlot from speaking of chastity.
stances.translation: A.J. Wensinck, Mystic Treatises by Isaac of Nineveh (Amsterdam, 1923)
stances.context: The next lines: 'Fire cannot burn fresh wood; the love of God cannot be kindled in a heart that loves comfort.' Treatise 60 praises chastity made splendid 'by the suffering of hunger'. Written in the late 7th century for solitaries.

stances.summary: Eating and sleeping are needs we should feel ashamed of, set beside the soul's calling. Antony lived on bread, salt and water and would rather not be seen eating.
stances.quote: And he used to eat and sleep, and go about all other bodily necessities with shame when he thought of the spiritual faculties of the soul.
stances.translation: H. Ellershaw, NPNF Second Series vol. 4, 1892
stances.context: This is Athanasius's account, written about 360 soon after Antony died, and Athanasius had met him. Section 7: 'His food was bread and salt, his drink, water only. Of flesh and wine it is superfluous even to speak.' Section 45 goes on: he often ate 'with the brethren; covered with shame on these occasions, yet speaking boldly words of help'. Compare his gentler side in the bow saying (claim a).

stances.summary: Gluttony fools us. The belly cries hunger when it is full, and it keeps inventing sauces and treats. The lover of food even looks forward to feast days for the menu.
stances.quote: Gluttony is hypocrisy of the belly: when it is full it cries out that it is in want, and when it is loaded and bursting it shouts that it is hungry. Gluttony is the inventor of seasonings, the fountain of sweet pleasures.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek (PG 88) as transcribed on Greek Wikisource
stances.original: Γαστριμαργία ἐστὶν κοιλίας ὑπόκρισις· κεκορεσμένη γὰρ οὖσα ἔνδειαν ἀναβοᾷ, καὶ πεφορημένη καὶ ῥηγνυμένη πεινᾷν ἀνακράζει. Γαστριμαργία ἐστὶν καρυκείας δημιουργός, ἡδυτήτων πηγή.
stances.context: The same step, own rendering: 'The Jew rejoices in Sabbath and feast; the gluttonous monk in Saturday and Sunday. He counts the days to Easter and gets the dishes ready days before.' Another line: for the perfect, a time of gladness means freedom from care, but for the passion-ridden it is 'a feast of feasts'. About 600, Sinai. Only modern English exists (copyrighted), so none is used.

stances.summary: Wine is really not for monks, but since modern monks cannot be persuaded, allow a measured amount and never drink to fullness. Two cooked dishes are enough, and overeating is the most un-Christian thing of all.
stances.quote: Indeed we read that wine is not suitable for monks at all. But because, in our day, it is not possible to persuade the monks of this, let us agree at least as to the fact that we should not drink till we are sated, but sparingly.
stances.translation: Ernest F. Henderson, Select Historical Documents of the Middle Ages (London: George Bell and Sons, 1910)
stances.original: Licet legamus vinum omnino monachorum non esse, sed quia nostris temporibus id monachis persuaderi non potest, saltim vel hoc consentiamus ut non usque ad satietatem bibamus, sed parcius (https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/benedict.html, which prints 'omnimo')
stances.context: The 'we read' points to the Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Poemen 19: 'Wine is not for monks at all'). Chapter 39 allows two cooked dishes, plus fruit or fresh vegetables if available, and a pound of bread: 'nothing is so contrary to every Christian as surfeiting.' The Rule is famously moderate by monastic standards, allowing a daily measure (hemina) of wine, and chapter 40 opens 'Each one has his own gift from God', so strength 1. About 530-540.

stances.summary: Clergy should stay away from dinner parties with outsiders. They breed a love of feasting and worldly talk, and your cup keeps being refilled.
stances.quote: Banquets with strangers engross one's attention, and soon produce a love for feasting.
stances.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, NPNF Second Series vol. 10, 1896
stances.work: On the Duties of the Clergy (De officiis ministrorum)
stances.context: It is addressed to clergy and presented as advice on modesty and reputation. He still insists they be 'hospitable to travellers'. Also: 'One's glass, too, even against one's will, is filled time after time.' His fuller treatment is the sermon On Elijah and Fasting (De Helia et ieiunio), which attacks drinking parties. No pre-1929 English was found online, so it is not quoted.

stances.summary: The fruits of the earth are there to keep us alive. Nature needs very little, and anything piled on beyond that is either unpleasant or harmful. The simple age before luxury was the happy one.
stances.quote: Doubtless the fruits of the earth are given for the sustenance of living creatures. But if thou art content to supply thy wants so far as suffices nature, there is no need to resort to fortune's bounty. Nature is content with few things, and with a very little of these.
stances.translation: H.R. James (London: Elliot Stock, 1897), Project Gutenberg text
stances.context: Lady Philosophy speaks, and Boethius the character accepts her teaching. The next poem (Book 2, poem 5, 'The Former Age') praises people who 'On frugal acorns sparely fed' and did not know how to mix honey into wine. Written in prison about 524. The argument is classical and philosophical rather than explicitly Christian, but Boethius was a Christian and wrote theological tractates. Plain-text file: compare after collapsing whitespace.

stances.summary: The best way is to eat every day, but a little less than your fill. The Fathers tried long fasts and found this light 'royal way' better. Wine is not for monks at all.
stances.quote: Abba Poemen said to him: I want the one who eats to eat every day, but a little short of his fill, so that he is not sated.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek alphabetical Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Cotelier text, PG 65)
stances.original: Λέγει αὐτῷ ὁ ἀββᾶς Ποιμήν· Ἐγὼ θέλω τὸν ἐσθίοντα καθ᾽ ἡμέραν παρὰ μικρὸν ἐσθίειν, ἵνα μὴ χορτάζηται.
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Apophthegmata Patrum), alphabetical collection
stances.context: Abba Joseph asked how one should fast. Poemen admits he once fasted for days or a week, 'and they found that it is better to eat every day, but a little; and they handed down to us the royal way, for it is light' (own rendering). Poemen 19, on the same page: told of a monk who did not drink wine, he said 'Wine does not belong to monks at all' (Ὁ οἶνος ὅλως οὐκ ἔστι τῶν μοναχῶν). This is the saying Benedict cites. Moderate, not severe, but aimed at not being filled rather than at enjoyment. The page's English is Ward's (copyrighted, not used).

stances.summary: The Gospel frees Christians to eat every kind of food, but that freedom gives no licence for luxury. God does not delight in our food, and the liberty comes with a law of frugality.
stances.quote: although in the Gospel the use of meats is universally given to us, yet it is understood to be given to us only with the law of frugality and continence.
stances.translation: Robert Ernest Wallis, ANF vol. 5, 1886
stances.context: Chapter 5: God is not 'careful for these pleasures, so as to rejoice in our food', and the true meat is 'a true faith, an unspotted conscience'. Chapter 6 opens: 'from the fact that liberty of meats is granted to us, it does not of necessity follow that luxury is allowed us'. He mocks Christians who drink wine while fasting in the early morning. Written about 250, after Novatian had become the rigorist anti-pope (schismatic).

stances.summary: Food and wine are God's works, and Christ Himself drank wine, against those who ban it. Christians may feast and drink sober cups of friendship. But food exists for health, not pleasure, so eat plainly and flee gourmet luxury.
stances.quote: But we, the people of peace, feasting for lawful enjoyment, not to wantonness, drink sober cups of friendship, that our friendships may be shown in a way truly appropriate to the name.
stances.translation: William Wilson, ANF vol. 2, 1885
stances.context: Same chapter: 'It is fitting, then, that some apply wine by way of physic, for the sake of health alone, and others for purposes of relaxation and enjoyment'. On Christ drinking wine he says: 'Let this be held fast by us against those that are called Encratites.' But chapter 1 says God provided 'food and drink, for sustenance, not for pleasure', and 'we should use them, without undue attachment'. He also says boys and girls should avoid wine and old men may drink 'more cheerfully'. Written about 190-200 for lay Christians. It is the fullest early Christian treatment of dinner-table manners.

stances.summary: Wine is God's good work, given to make us glad. Blame drunkenness, not wine. But even needed food and drink should be measured by real need, and Paul's 'a little wine' is closer to advice to abstain.
stances.quote: For wine was given us of God, not that we might be drunken, but that we might be sober; that we might be glad, not that we get ourselves pain.
stances.translation: W.R.W. Stephens, NPNF First Series vol. 9, 1889
stances.context: Same section: 'Let there be no drunkenness; for wine is the work of God, but drunkenness is the work of the devil.' He argues this against 'heretics, who speak evil of God's creatures' and against pious people who say 'Let there be no wine'. But the section opens by saying Paul's advice to Timothy 'rather amounts to a recommendation of abstinence'. Section 12 ends: 'we should always mete out even the needful meat and drink... by occasions and necessities'. Preached at Antioch in 387. Elsewhere he attacks luxury feasting hard. This is the nearest the great ascetic preachers come to 'meant to be enjoyed'.

stances.summary: On a holiday evening with a friend, spend the time in gladness, and let a sober meal ring with psalms. Luxurious banquets only torment the rich.
stances.quote: since this is a holiday rest, and a time of leisure, whatever remains of the day, now that the sun is sloping towards the evening, let us spend it in gladness, nor let even the hour of repast be without heavenly grace. Let the temperate meal resound with psalms
stances.translation: Robert Ernest Wallis, ANF vol. 5, 1886
stances.work: To Donatus (Ad Donatum), printed as Epistle 1 in ANF
stances.context: Written soon after his conversion, about 246. It pictures a glad, shared, temperate meal among friends. Earlier in the same work he describes the rich man who 'In the midst of the banquet... sighs, although he drinks from a jewelled goblet', calling such luxuries 'gilded torments'. So it is joy in company and sobriety, not delight in fine fare. Marked mixed.

stances.summary: Let newly converted peoples keep their festival feasts, killing animals to eat in praise of God and thanking Him for being filled. Outward joys can lead to inward ones. Still, the fault lies in desire, not food, and hunting out daintier food is a form of gluttony.
stances.quote: slay animals to the praise of God for their own eating, and return thanks to the Giver of all for their fullness, so that, while some joys are reserved to them outwardly, they may be able the more easily to incline their minds to inward joys.
stances.translation: James Barmby, NPNF Second Series vol. 13, 1898
stances.context: This is pastoral advice for the mission to the English, and the feasting is a stepping-stone ('one who strives to ascend to the highest place must needs rise by steps'), not an ideal. His own ascetic teaching is stricter. Moralia 30.18.60 (https://www.lectionarycentral.com/GregoryMoralia/Book30.html) lists five ways gluttony tempts, including seeking 'daintier food' and food 'prepared more carefully'. But it also says 'it is not the food, but the desire that is in fault. Whence also we frequently take some delicate fare without blame'. Pastoral Rule 3.19 warns the abstinent not to 'condemn the creature of God'.

stances.summary: Once a year, when the fruit was ripe, he asked for some and tasted a little of each kind, thanking God. It was a small, grateful tasting of God's gifts within a life of severe self-denial.
stances.quote: He also said that when he heard that every kind of fruit had ripened, he would say of his own accord: Bring me some. And he would taste a little from all of them, once only, giving thanks to God.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek alphabetical Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Cotelier text, PG 65)
stances.original: Εἶπε πάλιν, ὅτι ὡς ἤκουεν ὅτι ἐτελέσθη πᾶν γένος ὀπώρας, ἔλεγεν ἀφ᾽ ἑαυτοῦ· Φέρετέ μοι. Καὶ ἐγεύετο ἅπαξ μόνον ἀπὸ πάντων μικρόν, εὐχαριστῶν τῷ Θεῷ.
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Apophthegmata Patrum), alphabetical collection
stances.location: Arsenius 19 (Ward's numbering; the teller is Abba Daniel)
stances.context: This is a report about him, not his own words. The saying just before (Arsenius 18) shows the other side. He would not change the stinking water his palm leaves soaked in, saying (own rendering) 'instead of the incense and perfumes I enjoyed in the world, I must take this smell'. Arsenius had been a high official at the imperial court before becoming a monk at Scetis (died about 449). The page's English is Ward's (copyrighted, not used).

stances.summary: Eating and drinking belong to God's good creation and to the life to come. Christ promised to drink new wine with His disciples in the Kingdom, where God will set a table full of every kind of dish.
stances.quote: but shall have a table at hand prepared for them by God, supplying them with all sorts of dishes.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: He is speaking of the righteous in the coming kingdom, the 'true Sabbath'. Section 1 argues that Christ's promise to drink 'of the fruit of the vine' there must be meant literally, because 'to drink of that which flows from the vine pertains to flesh'. Section 3 passes on the elders' story, via Papias, of giant vines. This is about the goodness of food and wine in God's plan, aimed against the Gnostics' contempt for matter. It says nothing about enjoying fine food now, so strength 1. About 180.

stances.summary: Eating with thanksgiving is no worse than fasting. God made animals and wine for us to use, and Christ ate and drank freely, went to dinners and a wedding, and turned water into wine.
stances.quote: The Lord himself was called by the Pharisees a wine-bibber and a glutton, the friend of publicans and sinners, because he did not decline the invitation of Zacchæus to dinner, and went to the marriage-feast.
stances.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, NPNF Second Series vol. 6, 1893
stances.work: Jovinian's lost treatise, as quoted and summarised by Jerome in Against Jovinian
stances.context: Jovinian was a Roman monk. His writings survive only through a hostile witness, Jerome, who sets out Jovinian's arguments before attacking them ('Granted, he says...'). Treat the wording as Jerome's report. Book 1.3 gives Jovinian's thesis: 'there is no difference between abstinence from food and its reception with thanksgiving' (the New Advent summary gives it as 'Abstinence is no better than a thankful partaking of food'). The same passage: 'He did not make water, but wine... After the resurrection he ate a fish and part of a honey-comb, not sesame nuts and service-berries.' Jovinian was condemned at Rome under Siricius and at Milan under Ambrose (about 390-393). He is the clearest early voice for this claim. He is not in the results pool. Quote check: the page encodes 'æ' as an HTML entity.

stances.summary: A clergyman who refuses meat and wine on feast days because he thinks them unclean, rather than as a chosen discipline, insults God's good creation and should be deposed.
stances.quote: If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon, does not on festival days partake of flesh and wine, from an abhorrence of them, and not out of religious restraint, let him be deposed, as being seared in his own conscience, and being the cause of offense to many.
stances.translation: Henry R. Percival, NPNF Second Series vol. 14, 1900
stances.work: Apostolic Canons (the last chapter of the Apostolic Constitutions, book 8)
stances.context: Canon 51 also condemns clergy who abstain from marriage, flesh or wine 'as abhorring them, forgetting that God made all things very good'. This is church law, not a person. Its target is contempt for creation (Encratite or Manichaean), not a defence of gourmet pleasure. It does make feasting with meat and wine a duty on festivals. Include only as context, or as an anonymous voice.

splits_fathers: Laughter (a): the great majority are against laughter, and the voices are strongest for monks and clergy. Chrysostom, Basil, Ambrose, Benedict, Jerome, Gregory the Great, Isaac, and the desert sayings (Syncletica, Poemen, Pambo, Ammonas, John at the love-feast) all say this life is for weeping over sin. Chrysostom and Basil add that the Gospels never show Christ laughing, and Chrysostom calls play the devil's gift. The other side is real but small. None of them praises a loud belly laugh. They praise measured cheerfulness, wit and relaxation. Clement makes laughter natural, to be governed and not uprooted. Gregory of Nazianzus praises Basil's wit used in season. Augustine tells teachers to refresh a tired listener with 'honest cheerfulness'. Antony's bow saying and Cassian's John-and-the-partridge story defend unbending. Tertullian calls decent laughter at error a duty. Hermas calls cheerfulness pleasing to God. Climacus rejects bodily laughter but praises 'the laughter of the soul'. So the claim as worded, 'a good hearty laugh', would put almost every Father on 'disagree'. 'A bit of light-hearted fun is good for the soul' gets real voices on both sides. Food (b): almost all agree that food and wine are good creatures of God and must not be treated as unclean. Clement against the Encratites, Basil Long Rule 18, Chrysostom, Augustine, Gregory the Great and the Apostolic Canons all say so. But most deny that pleasure is the point. Clement ('for sustenance, not for pleasure'), Basil, Augustine ('take food as medicine'), Gregory of Nyssa, Lactantius (who poses the exact question and answers no), Boethius, Isaac and Climacus all take that line. Jerome, Tertullian as a Montanist, Antony and Gregory of Nazianzus press hard for abstinence. The real 'enjoy it' side: Jovinian ('abstinence is no better than a thankful partaking'; condemned), Chrysostom ('wine was given... that we might be glad'), Clement ('feasting for lawful enjoyment'), the Apostolic Canons (clergy must eat meat and drink wine on feasts), Gregory the Great (let the English keep feasting days), Irenaeus (the banquet of the Kingdom), and Cyprian (a glad, sober holiday meal). Sharpest real pairs: Jovinian against Jerome, Tertullian's Apology against his On Fasting, Clement against Lactantius, and Chrysostom on wine against Jerome on wine.
splits_people_today: Laughter (a): almost everyone today, Christian or not, agrees that laughter is good for you ('laughter is the best medicine' is a common saying, and Proverbs 17:22 is widely quoted). Only a small minority of very traditional, monastic-minded or naturally grave people would disagree. As worded, the claim is badly one-sided today and one-sided the other way among the Fathers, which is useful for a surprising reveal but tells the quiz little. It splits people better if sharpened. Try 'A truly serious person rarely laughs' or 'Joking has no place around holy things'. Many devout people and many cheerful people would part company on those. Food (b): most people today agree too (food culture and 'treat yourself'), perhaps 80% or more. Real dissent comes from people who say 'food is fuel' or 'I eat to live', from strict dieters and minimalists, and from Christians who take fasting seriously (Orthodox, traditional Catholics, some evangelicals). It splits better as 'Food is mainly fuel; enjoying it is beside the point' against 'A really good meal is one of life's great gifts'. That pairing roughly matches Basil and Augustine against Jovinian and Clement at his warmest.

misattributions.line: Eat to live, do not live to eat.
misattributions.truth: Clement does write it (Paedagogus 2.1: 'Some men, in truth, live that they may eat... But the Instructor enjoins us to eat that we may live'), but he is reusing an old proverb that ancient writers credited to Socrates. Credit Clement for using it, not for coining it.

misattributions.line: Jesus never laughed (quoted flatly as the words of Chrysostom or Basil).
misattributions.truth: Both hedge. Chrysostom (Homily 6 on Matthew): Christ is seen weeping 'but nowhere laugh, nay, nor smile but a little; no one at least of the evangelists has mentioned this', and 'these things I say, not to suppress all laughter'. Basil (Long Rules 17): the Lord seems never to have laughed 'so far as we may judge from the narrative of the gospels'. Neither says it as an outright fact, so do not print it as a bare quotation.

misattributions.line: Wine is not for monks at all.
misattributions.truth: Benedict cites it ('we read') from the Sayings of the Desert Fathers, where it is Abba Poemen's saying (Poemen 19). Benedict himself allows a daily measure of wine.

misattributions.line: The hunter and the bow: 'If you bend the bow too far it breaks, and so will the brothers.'
misattributions.attributed_to: Antony the Great (or John the Evangelist)
misattributions.truth: The same parable is told of two men: of Antony in the Greek alphabetical Sayings (Antony 13, compiled late 5th century) and of St John the Evangelist in Cassian, Conference 24.21. Neither comes from the person's own writing. Present it as 'a story told of Antony', not as his written teaching.

notes: Quote checking: every quote marked own_rendering false was checked by script against the page at its url, after removing tags, decoding HTML entities (New Advent writes æ as æ), straightening curly quotes and dashes, and collapsing whitespace. New Advent pages leave double spaces where footnote links sit, and the archive.org and Gutenberg plain texts break lines mid-sentence, so any machine check must collapse whitespace. The five own renderings (Syncletica, Poemen x2, Antony's bow saying, Arsenius, Climacus x2) come from the Greek, because the only English on those pages is Benedicta Ward's copyrighted translation, and for Climacus only modern English exists. Most of the anti-laughter texts are addressed to monks, nuns or clergy (Basil's Rules, Benedict, Ambrose's De officiis, Jerome to consecrated virgins, the desert sayings). The quiz should not present them as rules for everyone without saying so. Clement, writing for lay families, is the clearest lay voice and the clearest middle. The tradition links the two claims: Gregory the Great makes 'foolish mirth' an offspring of gluttony. Good ironies for a reveal: Jerome, the fiercest satirist, told Demetrias to leave laughing to worldlings. Basil forbade laughter, yet Gregory of Nazianzus praised his wit. Tertullian described the Christian love-feast warmly in 197 and mocked it as a Montanist. Heterodox or condemned: Tertullian (Montanist period), Novatian (schismatic), Jovinian (condemned about 390-393). Pool members looked for but not recorded, because no public-domain or verifiable text was found: Evagrius (no pre-1929 English and no Greek text reached), Ephrem (the Nativity and Epiphany hymns in NPNF celebrate feasts but say nothing on enjoying food or on laughter), Hilary, Pelagius (the Letter to Demetrias exists only in modern English), Paulinus of Nola (Carmen 27 tolerates peasants feasting at St Felix's shrine as a forgivable error, but no Latin or pre-1929 English was reached to verify), Macrina (the Life of Macrina, Lowther Clarke 1916, https://www.tertullian.org/fathers/gregory_macrina_1_life.htm, says only that on her deathbed 'in every way she tried to be cheerful'), Perpetua (the martyrs' 'Go and play' in Saturus's vision is heavenly, not a stance), Moses the Black (Moses 5: he broke a community fast to cook for visiting brothers, and the clergy said he had broken a human command to keep God's. That is hospitality over rules, not enjoyment, but it may suit a hospitality question), Athanasius (only as author of the Life of Antony), and Ignatius, Justin, Origen and Hippolytus (nothing found). Further anti-laughter sayings in Budge's Paradise vol. 2 (1907), same archive.org file as the Pambo entry: Abba Ammon, 'Laugh not, O brother, for if thou dost, thou wilt drive the fear of God out of thy soul' (no. 143, split by a page break in the OCR). Abba Sinu (in the Greek, John) wept when a brother laughed at the love-feast (no. 139). An old man: 'Laughter and familiar talking are like unto the fire which kindleth among the reeds' (no. 283). The Council of Gangra (about 340) also anathematised people who condemn those who eat meat with faith, but a council is not a person. My web-search allowance ran out near the end, so Gregory of Nyssa's Homilies on Ecclesiastes ('a time to laugh') and the Greek of Evagrius were not checked.
